paras: The attempted lynching of Bob Harris took place in Des Moines, Iowa, on the night of September 16, 1882, when a crowd of several hundred to perhaps 1,500 men rushed the county jail to hang a prisoner accused of beating and robbing the grocer John B. James. Sheriff Littleton had already sent Harris out of the city, and the crowd searched the jail, the courthouse and the state arsenal without finding him. Papers across the country carried the story as a frustrated case of "lynch law", and in December Harris was convicted and sentenced to the penitentiary.

Des Moines had seen a run of violent robberies in the days before, including the killing of Henry Scribner and an assault on saloon keeper Hans Kastberg, all said to have been made with an iron fish plate. On the afternoon of Saturday, September 16, a stranger struck James on the head in his grocery at Twelfth and Sycamore streets, fracturing his skull. James's clerk returned with the delivery wagon and chased the man through the streets, and after a run of over a mile he was stopped by a policeman at a downtown saloon and jailed.

The prisoner gave his name as Bob Harris and was described as over six feet tall and athletic, with black hair and a dark beard; no report gives his race. Wire reports said he had robbed James of $900, while the detailed Des Moines accounts say he fled when the clerk arrived, and one German-language version says he took nothing.

By 8 p.m. the streets were filled with men urging that the assailant be hanged, and a meeting of "law-abiding citizens" was called to find speakers to dissuade a mob. About the same hour the sheriff sent Harris away in a carriage under two guards, who were reportedly ordered to shoot him if he tried to escape. City authorities closed the saloons at nine, which, according to the New Haven Morning Journal and Courier, only turned more men into the streets, and about a thousand had gathered at the courthouse by ten.

The crowd then rushed the jail in the courthouse basement and demanded the prisoner. Sheriff Littleton mounted a box and pledged his honor that Harris was gone, and, fearing the doors would be battered down, let a committee chosen by the crowd search the cells; one of its members had helped capture Harris. When the committee found nothing, the crowd searched the rest of the courthouse and then went to the state arsenal, returning to hang about the jail in the belief that he was hidden in a county office vault. Most of the crowd had left by midnight, though the St. Paul Daily Globe reported that it stayed until 2 a.m. and a small group until daylight.

Harris's guards reached the Winterset jail, about forty miles away, at 4 a.m., and the next afternoon Sheriff Littleton drove him on to Greenfield in Adair County. Members of the crowd, among them business men of the city, said they would try again when Harris was brought back for trial. No arrest of anyone in the crowd is reported in the coverage.

James survived his injuries for at least several weeks; a visitor reported in October that he was still bedridden but might recover. In December Harris was convicted of the assaults on James and Kastberg, and Judge McKenry, fearing mob violence, moved up the sentencing and gave him ten years on each charge at the Fort Madison penitentiary.

No Black newspaper coverage from 1882 was available, and the episode is known from white papers that ran the Des Moines dispatches from Minnesota and Wisconsin to Georgia, Texas and Washington within a week. The St. Paul Daily Globe headlined it "Mobbish Iowans" and "Mob Law in Iowa", the New-York Tribune "Hunted by a Mob" and the Dallas Daily Herald "Lynch Law Frustrated". Most papers called the accused "the villain" or "a thug" and printed the assault on James at more length than the mob.

Several accounts treated the crowd sympathetically: the Omaha Bee's correspondent wrote that public sentiment seemed to "justify and excuse the demonstrations", and the Wheeling Register said the business men in the crowd had acted to "quell the reign of lawlessness". A Wisconsin weekly later summed up the case by saying Des Moines would clear out its cut-throats "even if it takes mob law to do it." The case drew special notice in Mineral Point, Wisconsin, where James had grown up and where two papers followed his condition and Harris's removal.

Estimates of the crowd differ widely: one wire version gave 150 men and a search committee of two, the New Haven account about a thousand and a committee of three, and the longer wire 1,000 or 1,500 and a committee of ten. Early reports placed Harris at Indianola or Adel, while a later Des Moines dispatch, giving times and route, placed him at Winterset and then Greenfield.

reader.title: Attempted lynching of Bob Harris
chips: Lynching of any race (not in the anti-Black count)
bases: A crowd went to the Des Moines jail to take and hang a prisoner accused of assault and robbery, and failed only because the sheriff had sent him away (A1, A11, A21).

A crowd of hundreds to over a thousand sought to hang Harris for the assault on James, but he had been removed and no one was killed (A1, A11, A37); it was an attempted lynching. No report gives Harris's race or a racial motive, so whether it was anti-Black violence is not shown.
Separate wire versions (A1, A7), a detailed special (A11, A18) and later dispatches (A23, A37) agree that a crowd demanded Harris at the jail and searched for him without finding him.

accounts.label: Short wire version
accounts.gist: A crowd of 150 demanded Harris; a committee of two who knew him searched the jail, and the crowd searched the neighborhood till daylight.

accounts.label: Des Moines special correspondent
accounts.gist: About a thousand gathered after the saloons closed; a committee of three searched; many of the best citizens and business men vowed to try again when Harris returned for trial.

accounts.label: Officials' version of the removal
accounts.gist: Officials said Harris had been sent out under guard with orders to shoot him if he tried to escape; later reports put him at Winterset and then Greenfield.

framing.detail: The St. Paul Daily Globe headlined 'Mobbish Iowans' and 'Mob Law in Iowa' but called the accused 'the villain' and the assault 'Deadly'.
The Omaha Bee's Des Moines correspondent wrote that public sentiment seemed to 'justify and excuse' the demonstrations.

The Wheeling Register said the business men in the crowd had resorted to it 'to quell the reign of lawlessness'; the River Falls Journal said Des Moines would clear out cut-throats 'even if it takes mob law'.
Dallas headlined 'Lynch Law Frustrated' and the New-York Tribune 'Hunted by a Mob', printing the wire without comment.

conflicts.note: The detailed accounts (A11, A12) say he ran when the clerk arrived and mention no money taken; A14 says so explicitly.
The Sept. 18 dispatch (A23) is later and specific, giving the 4 a.m. arrival at Winterset and the sheriff's onward drive.

versions.value: remained till 2 a.m., a small gang till daylight

record_check.dossier: No report gives Harris's race or calls the episode racial; the only description is 'black hair, and dark, stubby beard'. Inclusion as anti-Black violence is unsupported by these papers.
Reports range from 150 to 1,000 or 1,500 (one OCR reads 10,000 or 15,000); 1,900 appears nowhere.
The pursuit was the clerk and citizens chasing the fleeing man before his arrest; the mob's acts were a rush on the jail, a committee search, and searches of the arsenal and courthouse.

record_check.record: accused of assaulting and robbing grocer John James
record_check.dossier: Accused of assault with intent to rob; whether anything was taken is disputed.
'Bob Harris' was the name he gave; Mineral Point papers print 'Rob Harris'.
Harris was lodged at Winterset and Greenfield, convicted of two assaults, and sentenced to ten years on each at Fort Madison.
